runs.text: Lead service line need is not one problem
States face different mixes of identification and replacement work
Act on known Lead and GRR lines
Comparing states on only one measure would hide where their actual workload sits.
Scope: 43,993 complete-report Community Water Systems across 50 states and DC

Source: U.S. EPA 2026 Q2 Service Line Inventory. Analytical source: completed Lead_Service_Line_Analysis.ipynb and outputs/state_service_line_summary.csv. Known Replacement Inventory = Lead + GRR. Identification Need = Lead Status Unknown, not confirmed lead. Complete-report Community Water Systems only. No composite ranking. Population comparisons use 2025 Census state resident population for the 2026 Q2 inventory.
Most of the reported national workload

Replacement and identification needs do not consistently move together.
One overall “need” ranking would hide these differences.
Planning should distinguish known replacement work from inventory still requiring identification.
This pattern describes inventory. It does not measure progress, maturity, or cause.
Source: U.S. EPA 2026 Q2 Service Line Inventory. Each point represents one state or DC.

State size changes who stands out,
and local evidence is needed before acting
Raw totals show where the largest overall inventories are concentrated.
Rhode Island, Louisiana and New Mexico become more visible.
State inventories can guide deeper local investigation.
Intervention decisions require utility-level records, GIS information, inspections, funding information, local capacity, project plans and other local evidence.
How do state and utility identification and replacement needs align with available funding and local capacity to complete service-line replacement?
Unknown does not mean lead. Inventory does not measure exposure or water quality. Incomplete-report systems are excluded.
Sources: U.S. EPA 2026 Q2 Service Line Inventory; U.S. Census Bureau 2025 resident population estimates (population context).
